patient_name: OET role-play — mother of a teenager with peanut allergy, frightened of using the adrenaline auto-injector wrongly
chief_complaint: Teach a frightened mother when and how to use an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector for her son's peanut allergy, and what to do afterwards

team_brief.title: Anaphylaxis: a mother afraid of 'doing it wrong' with the auto-injector
team_brief.patient: Chidi Eze, 14-year-old boy with a peanut allergy (present in the waiting room); the conversation is with his mother, Mrs Chioma Eze
team_brief.location: Allergy clinic; you are the allergy nurse and you are talking to Chidi's mother
team_brief.situation: Last month Chidi had a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) after eating a snack containing peanuts at a party, and was treated in the emergency department. He has now been prescribed adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injectors. His mother has come to learn how to use them, but she says she is terrified of doing it wrong.
background: During the reaction his lips and tongue swelled, he was wheezy, his voice was hoarse and he vomited. A friend's parent called an ambulance.
He also has mild asthma, which increases the risk of a severe reaction.
He is starting at a new school next week.
current_status: Two adrenaline auto-injectors have been prescribed, plus a training device without a needle.
key_data: Use the auto-injector straight away for signs of a severe reaction: swelling of the tongue or throat, difficulty swallowing, a hoarse voice, wheeze or difficulty breathing, feeling faint, very pale or floppy, or collapse. If in doubt, give it.
Hives, itching or a tingly mouth on their own are signs of a mild reaction: follow the allergy action plan (usually an antihistamine), stay with him and watch closely for any severe sign.

How to use (follow the device leaflet): hold it in a fist, remove the safety cap, press the tip firmly into the outer thigh (it can go through clothing) until it clicks, hold it in place for the time stated on the device, then remove it.

Afterwards: call the emergency number and say 'anaphylaxis'. Lie him down with his legs raised, or let him sit up if breathing is difficult; do not let him stand or walk. If he is no better after 5 minutes (or the time given in his allergy action plan), use the second auto-injector. He must go to hospital even if he feels better.

Adrenaline is a hormone the body makes naturally. It may cause shaking, a fast heartbeat or paleness for a short time; this is expected. The risk of not giving it in a severe reaction is much greater than the risk of giving it.
Two auto-injectors should be with Chidi at all times; he should carry them himself, and the school needs a copy of his allergy action plan.
treatments: Already done: allergy testing confirmed peanut allergy; auto-injectors and a written allergy action plan prescribed.
Pending: Chidi's own training session; school allergy plan.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Mrs Eze's fears, explain when and how to use the auto-injector, and advise her what to do after using it.
must_include: Find out what Mrs Eze already knows and what frightens her about using the auto-injector.
Explain the signs of a severe allergic reaction that mean the auto-injector should be used straight away.
Explain step by step how to use the auto-injector, using the training device.
Advise her what to do after using it (emergency call, position, second dose, hospital).
Reassure her that the medicine is safe to give if in doubt, and advise that Chidi should always carry two auto-injectors.

kickoff_text: Hello. I'll be honest, I'm dreading this. What if I stick it in wrong and hurt him?
persona_override: You are Chioma Eze, a 44-year-old mother of Chidi, 14, who had a severe allergic reaction to peanuts at a party last month. You are warm, talkative when nervous, and frightened. Your specific fear: that in a panic you will 'do it wrong' — inject in the wrong place, hurt him, or give adrenaline when he does not really need it and 'damage his heart'. Because of this, you have been thinking you would rather just call an ambulance and wait. Ground truth: at the party his lips and tongue swelled, he was wheezy, his voice went hoarse and he was sick; another parent called an ambulance; he has mild asthma and uses an inhaler; he starts a new school next week; he is embarrassed and does not want to carry the pens in his bag; you have the two auto-injectors and the training pen in a bag but have not opened them; you are not sure whether hives on their own mean you should use it. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words like 'anaphylaxis', 'epinephrine', 'intramuscular', 'anterolateral thigh', 'biphasic reaction' or 'allergen' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse goes straight into the technique without asking what frightens you, follow along, then say more anxiously: 'But what if I give it and he didn't need it? Could it hurt his heart?' If the nurse reassures you that adrenaline is a natural hormone, that side effects like shaking pass quickly, and that it is safer to give it if in doubt, calm down a little: 'So it's worse not to give it?' Then ask one follow-up: 'How do I know it's bad enough?' When the technique is explained, practise with the trainer and describe what you are doing; make one mistake (for example, putting your thumb over the end or saying you would inject into his arm) so there is something to correct. If the nurse does not mention what to do afterwards, ask near the end: 'And once I've done it, is that it?' If asked, mention that Chidi does not want to carry the pens. Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: say you feel more confident, that you will practise with Chidi tonight, and thank the nurse.
learning_objectives: find out what the parent knows and what frightens her about the auto-injector
explain the signs of a severe allergic reaction that mean use the auto-injector straight away
teach step by step: remove the safety cap, press into the outer thigh, hold in place
advise afterwards: call the emergency number, lie him down, second auto-injector after 5 minutes if no better, go to hospital
reassure that if in doubt, give the adrenaline
advise that he should always carry two auto-injectors and share the plan with school
suggested_questions: Lots of parents feel exactly the same, so you're not alone. Can you tell me what worries you most about using it?
If Chidi has any swelling of his tongue or throat, a hoarse voice, wheezing or trouble breathing, or he feels faint, use it straight away — don't wait to see if it gets better.
Let's practise with the trainer. Hold it in your fist, take off the safety cap, and push the tip firmly into the outside of his thigh until you hear a click, then hold it there.
Adrenaline is something our bodies make naturally. He may feel shaky for a little while, but if you're not sure, it's much safer to give it than not to.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Teaching a parent to recognise anaphylaxis and use an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guidance, NHS anaphylaxis information and ASCIA (Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy) anaphylaxis action plans; device technique follows the manufacturer's instructions and the child's written allergy action plan
core_concepts: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction affecting the airway, breathing or circulation; intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment and should not be delayed.
Fear of injecting wrongly or of side effects is a common reason carers delay adrenaline; delay is associated with worse outcomes.
Teenagers are at higher risk of fatal reactions, partly because they may not carry their auto-injectors; asthma increases risk further.
diagnostic_clues: A carer who plans to 'just call an ambulance and wait' may be avoiding the auto-injector out of fear.
Hives or itching alone usually indicate a mild reaction, but any airway, breathing or circulation sign means adrenaline is needed.
common_misconceptions: Adrenaline should be kept for when the child collapses.
Antihistamines or the asthma reliever can be used instead of adrenaline in a severe reaction.
If the child feels better after the injection, there is no need to go to hospital.
dangerous_errors: Advising the parent to wait and see, or to give an antihistamine first, when there are breathing or circulation signs.
Teaching injection into the arm, or holding the device with a thumb over the tip.
Advising the child to stand up or walk after a severe reaction, or omitting the need for hospital assessment.
management_principles: Explore the carer's fears and knowledge, then teach recognition, technique and aftercare in small steps.
Practise hands-on with a trainer device and correct errors using teach-back.
Emphasise 'if in doubt, give it', carrying two devices at all times, and sharing the written action plan with school.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Auto-injector technique (hold time, whether to massage the site) differs between devices; follow the manufacturer's leaflet.
The interval before a second dose (commonly 5 minutes), positioning advice and the emergency number follow the national guideline and the child's allergy action plan.
Dose strength depends on weight and the prescription; school policies on carrying and storing auto-injectors vary.
